content: If it is not feasible to establish a database containing individual patient data for those infected with HBV or HCV, healthcare workers at medical facilities can instead report aggregated data. This includes the total number of individuals tested, diagnosed, initiated on treatment, and those who have achieved viral suppression or cure. This core set of aggregated data can be compiled at subnational and national levels to create cascades of care. However, the use of aggregated data has limitations, as it does not allow for tracking individuals who move between facilities, nor does it enable deduplication. Consequently, the cascade generated is not an epidemiological cohort, and this limitation must be considered when interpreting the results of the analysis. Additionally, disaggregated analyses are restricted by the level of disaggregation available in the reporting tools, such as geographical or sociodemographic data, which can be critical for program management by identifying disparities in service coverage and quality. Despite these limitations, the core set of data from programmatic cascades of care can still be reported in an aggregated format at the national level using computer platforms, following the analysis plan proposed by WHO. The Global Hepatitis Programme has developed a generic application based on the District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2) software, which can be provided to countries upon request. Once data are reported at the national level, they can subsequently be submitted to WHO through the Global Reporting System on Hepatitis, which also utilizes a DHIS2 application. The stages of a hepatitis program cycle include initial assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation. During the initial assessment phase, obtaining baseline estimates of HBV and HCV prevalence is essential for setting priorities. Data extraction along the 10 core indicators can provide an overview of the baseline situation, including the availability of policies and plans, which document the level of national commitment. WHO conducted a survey on these indicators in 2017, and they are now collected annually as part of the Global Reporting System on Hepatitis. The assessment phase may also include an analysis of the national health information system's capacity to collect, analyze, disseminate, and use data for hepatitis elimination. At the planning stage, estimating the size of the population requiring treatment is critical for resource allocation. Core interventions for preventing viral hepatitis have been shown to be cost-effective or cost-saving. For testing and treatment, country-specific cost-effectiveness analyses from a healthcare perspective, along with budget impact analyses, can support the inclusion of these interventions in national health benefit packages under Universal Health Coverage. Input parameters for such analyses include the costs of diagnostics, medicines, and monitoring, as well as the annual costs of managing sequelae such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Online calculators can estimate the net cost of HBV and HCV treatment, accounting for future savings from prevented sequelae, and express results in terms of cost per healthy life year gained. In most lowand middle-income countries with access to affordable, high-quality generic HBV and HCV medicines, treatment is highly cost-effective or cost-saving from a healthcare perspective. During the implementation stage, countries must report and utilize domestically generated data to identify disparities in service coverage and quality and address programmatic gaps systematically and in a prioritized manner. Progress can also be reported internationally to WHO through the Global Reporting System for Hepatitis. At the final evaluation stage, the framework with the full set of 10 core indicators can document the result chain, with a particular focus on the impact in terms of incidence and mortality. Mathematical modeling can complement empirically collected data in several areas, such as estimating the prevalence of HBsAg in the general population and children under five, determining the incidence of HCV infection using biomarker data or trends from enhanced case reporting, estimating current mortality from past HBV and HCV infections using vital registration and sequelae surveillance data, and analyzing the cost and impact of various service coverage options on national viral hepatitis elimination plans. Viral hepatitis elimination requires the implementation of core interventions coordinated across different health programs and services. Strategic information for elimination efforts must be consolidated within the health information system to provide a comprehensive picture that guides hepatitis elimination at all stages of the program. While the strategic information system described may seem ambitious, countries can begin with simple elements and build upon them within the context of their national health information systems. WHO is available to provide technical assistance as needed.
